nameStory: The lake trout gets its straightforward name from its preferred home - the deep, cold lakes of northern regions. Unlike many trout that spend time in streams, this fish is a true lake dweller, earning it the nickname 'laker' among anglers who seek them in the depths.
description: The lake trout is a large, deep-bodied char that calls New England's coldest, deepest lakes home. These impressive fish can grow quite large, with their torpedo-shaped bodies built for life in deep water. They have a distinctive forked tail and typically display a gray-green coloration with pale spots scattered across their sides. As members of the char family, they're actually more closely related to brook trout than to true trout species.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to dark gray body with light cream or yellowish spots scattered across the sides - the spots are typically lighter than the body color, unlike the darker spots on many trout

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, robust body with a torpedo shape designed for deep water living - feels solid and heavy for its length when handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Deeply forked tail fin and white leading edges on the lower fins (pelvic, anal, and pectoral fins) that feel firm to the touch

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth extending past the eye with sharp teeth that you can feel if you run your finger carefully along the jaw line

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Generally larger than brook trout, with adults commonly reaching 15-20 inches and having a substantial, muscular feel when held

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found almost exclusively in deep, cold lakes - if you're catching fish in shallow water or streams, it's probably not a lake trout

habitat: Lake trout inhabit the deepest, coldest lakes in northern New England, particularly in Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont. They prefer lakes with plenty of deep water (often 100+ feet) and cold temperatures year-round, typically found in association with other cold-water species. These fish stick to the depths during warm months, only venturing into shallower areas when water temperatures drop.

seasonality.spring: Lake trout move into slightly shallower areas as ice melts, but still remain in deeper water than most other fish species. This is when they're most active after the long winter.
seasonality.summer: Retreat to the deepest, coldest parts of lakes as surface temperatures warm. Rarely found in water less than 40-50 feet deep during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Spawning season brings lake trout into shallower rocky areas, making them more accessible to anglers. Look for them over rocky reefs and shoals in October and November.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under ice in deep water, though they may move slightly shallower than their summer depths as the entire water column cools.

funFact: Lake trout can live for over 40 years and don't even start reproducing until they're 6-10 years old - making them the slow-growing giants of New England's cold lakes, with some individuals potentially older than the people trying to catch them!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large brook trout, but lake trout have light spots on a dark body (brook trout have dark spots on a lighter body) and lack the brook trout's distinctive worm-like markings on the back. Remember: lake trout live in LAKES and have LIGHT spots.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'trout,' lake trout are actually chars - the same group as brook trout and Arctic char. This naming confusion exists because early settlers called any salmon-like fish a 'trout,' regardless of their actual scientific relationships. In some areas, dark-colored lake trout caught from deep water are nicknamed 'mud hens' by local anglers.
compareHints: Lake trout are much larger and more robust than their char cousin, the brook trout, and live exclusively in deep lakes rather than streams. While brook trout have intricate worm-like patterns on their backs and red spots with blue halos, lake trout display a simpler pattern of light yellowish spots on a gray-green background. Lake trout also have a more deeply forked tail compared to the brook trout's square or slightly forked tail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Brook trout differ from their close relative the lake trout by being much smaller and more colorful, with those distinctive red spots that lake trout lack.
